newsitem.title: FRANCE: French hospital doctors march to salvage strike.
newsitem.headline: French hospital doctors march to salvage strike.

text.p: Striking French junior hospital doctors led a march of thousands Sunday to Bastille square in Paris to protest against government plans to reduce health spending.

The strikers, who had hoped to rally 40,000 demonstrators from across the country, claimed 50,000 took part in the march, backed by some general practitioners trade unions. Police had no early estimate of numbers.

Political commentators saw the demonstration as a last-ditch attempt to salvage a protest that has been losing steam in the past week in the face of the government's determination to cut the state deficit to join the European Union's planned single currency in 1999.
Unions said before the weekend that 19 out of 26 teaching hospitals were still on strike, while the government put the figure at 17 and the percentage of strikers at 19 percent.
"This is not a gallant last-stand. It is a historical turning point," the strikers' spokesman, Gilbert Zakine, told reporters during the good-humoured march.
"Wage earners are joining us in increasing numbers as they realise that our struggle against the rationing of medical care is a just one," he said.

The strikers, demanding wide-ranging talks with the government on the welfare reform, have called a "health blackout" on Monday, the second time this month they ask all doctors to join them in giving only emergency care.
Junior hospital doctors are protesting against state plans to fine doctors exceeding pre-set spending targets in order to plug the gaping welfare deficit.
In an unconnected protest, some 300 activists staged a sit-in at the Versailles palace, outside Paris, for a few hours to protest against poverty and record unemployment, police said.
They hung outside the former royal bedroom a banner reading "No palace life for the poor."
In another labour dispute, a five-day-old strike by cockpit crew forced airlines TAT and Air Liberte, French units of British Airways, to cancel three quarters of their weekend flights.
Pilots and flight engineers say pay and working conditions will be damaged by a merger of the two airlines.
